aspectTitle: F10 cross-format / embedded-application trap (iframe, object, embed, plug-in, shadow-DOM widget) — the SC's central and only mapped failure technique
aspectDescription: F10 is the single failure technique mapped to 2.1.2 and it describes the SC's archetypal scenario: keyboard focus enters embedded or cross-format content and cannot be moved back out to the host document. Every ACT case simulates traps with inline JS onblur/onkeydown on bare native <button>s in one document; ZERO cases contain an <iframe>, <object>, <embed>, applet, web-component/Shadow-DOM widget, or any document/format boundary. The human-judgment surface: deciding whether focus that has entered an embedded boundary can return to the parent, whether the embedded content provides an exit, and
scenario: SaaS onboarding coachmark embedded as a cross-document <iframe src='case-01-frame.html'>. The embedded mini-app's only control, a 'Got it' button, swallows Tab (keydown preventDefault + self-refocus) and re-grabs focus onblur, so focus enters the iframe and can never cross back to the parent's 'Open dashboard' link. No Esc, no exit advice.
mechanism: F10 cross-document iframe boundary: a capture-phase keydown on Tab inside the embedded document calls preventDefault() and re-focuses the only button, plus a blur->focus() re-grab. The host never receives the boundary-crossing focus event, so a keyboard user cannot return to the parent document. Verified via CDP: 26 Tab presses never reach the AFTER link; Esc does not free focus.

scenario: Nonprofit donation page with a hosted-card-fields-style payment widget in a cross-document <iframe>. The embedded form re-implements its own tab cycle: the last control ('Donate $25') loops forward Tab back to the first field, and Shift+Tab from the first field loops to the last, so Tab cycles among the widget's controls forever and never crosses the iframe boundary to the parent's 'Cancel and return to home' link. No exit advice.
mechanism: F10 / violation of G21 sufficient mechanism #1: instead of letting Tab exit after the final control, keydown handlers on the first and last embedded controls cancel Tab/Shift+Tab and re-cycle focus within the iframe. The forward-Tab loop at the cross-document boundary is never released. Verified via CDP: 26 Tab presses never leave the iframe; Esc does not free focus.

scenario: Forum thread reply box implemented as a custom element <comment-composer> whose UI lives in an open Shadow DOM (attachShadow mode:open, delegatesFocus:true). The light-DOM source is just the empty custom-element tag. The component listens for focusout on its shadow root and synchronously re-focuses the textarea, so Tab/Shift+Tab cycle textarea<->button forever and never cross the shadow boundary to the parent's 'Back to all threads' link. No Esc, no advice.
mechanism: F10 applied to a Shadow-DOM boundary: a focusout listener on the shadow root checks whether the new focus target is outside the root and, if so, re-focuses the textarea, preventing focus from ever leaving the shadow tree. The trap is invisible in light-DOM source. Verified via CDP (piercing the open shadow root): 26 Tab presses oscillate only between #ta and #post; the AFTER link is never reached and Esc does not free focus.

Inside the textarea Tab is deliberately captured to insert indentation (the WCAG rich-text-editor example), so plain Tab does not advance focus. BUT a persistent visible instruction inside the shadow root says 'Press Esc to leave the editor', and a working Esc handler blurs the textarea and moves focus across the shadow boundary to the host 'Publish' button. aspectTitle: Modal-dialog / popover focus restriction: legitimate containment vs. an undismissable trap (the Understanding carve-out)
aspectDescription: The Understanding explicitly states that intentional focus restriction inside a modal dialog or popover does NOT fail the SC, AS LONG AS the user knows how to untrap and leave. Trusted Tester Test 4.C reinforces this: focus SHOULD remain within a modal until it is closed, but you must check for traps WITHIN it. This poses a pure human-judgment question the corpus never asks: is a focus-cycling dialog a CONFORMANT modal (a discoverable, keyboard-operable dismiss — Esc, or a reachable Cancel/Close button) or a TRAP (no keyboard-reachable way to close, a non-functional close, or a focus cycle tha
scenario: Healthcare patient-portal refill modal built with native <dialog open>: a JS focus trap cycles Tab among the refill form's four controls, but there is no Close/Cancel control and no Esc handler. Because the dialog was rendered with the open attribute (not opened via showModal()) the UA's native Esc-cancel is not armed either; only a mouse backdrop-click escapes. Keyboard users are stranded.
mechanism: Focus is restricted to a modal whose cycle contains no keyboard-operable dismiss: the keydown handler early-returns for every key except Tab (so Esc is dead), the dialog has no Close/Cancel to tab to, and <dialog open> (vs showModal()) leaves the UA Esc-cancel inactive. The sole escape is a mouse backdrop mousedown, useless to keyboard/switch/magnifier users.

scenario: Government DMV vehicle-registration renewal modal (role=dialog aria-modal=true). Focus IS restricted to the dialog (Tab wraps among its controls), but this is the legitimate-containment carve-out: a wired, functional Esc handler closes the dialog and restores focus to the triggering button, and the focus cycle explicitly includes the focusable header Close (✕) and footer Cancel. Focus is contained (correct modal behavior per TT 4.C) yet always escapable.

scenario: E-commerce (outdoor retail) product 'Quick view' modal (role=dialog aria-modal=true). A focus trap cycles Tab among the size/quantity/Add-to-cart controls. The only dismiss is a round '✕' that is a <span> with role=button + aria-label and an onclick handler only — not focusable (no tabindex, not a real button) and with no keydown; there is also no Esc handler. scenario: Insurance quote wizard with two STACKED modals. The base 'Get a quote' modal is conformant in isolation (Esc closes, Close in cycle, focus restore). From inside it the user opens a top 'Discard this quote?' confirmation modal. The defect is the nested-dismiss handoff: pressing Esc on the top modal closes it but drops focus to <body> (it omits the focus-restore call), and the still-armed base trap re-grabs the next Tab, snapping focus back to the base modal's first field — a re-trap instead of an orderly return.
mechanism: Broken focus handoff across stacked layers: closeConfirm() removes the top scrim but omits confirmOpener.focus(), so dismissing the confirm modal collapses focus to <body>; the base-layer focusin guard then yanks focus to #zip on the next Tab (verified: Esc->body, Tab->#zip). The keyboard user cannot return in an orderly way to where they were and is re-trapped in the base modal — the exit from the stack is broken even though each modal is escapable alone.

aspectTitle: Esc and other platform 'standard exit methods' as the untrap mechanism — and whether they actually fire
aspectDescription: The Understanding names Esc as a commonly-used standard exit method and notes other platform-specific standard methods may exist; crucially, if focus can be moved away using a STANDARD exit method, NO advice is required — the advice clause only triggers for non-standard methods. Every scripted custom-exit case in the corpus uses Ctrl+M, a non-standard combo that always requires advice. The corpus therefore never tests the judgment call of whether a given key counts as a standard exit method (so no advice is owed), nor whether an Esc-based exit actually works. A human must (a) decide a key qual
scenario: Government public-library 'Renew library card' modal. Focus is contained (Tab cycles inside), there is NO advice text and the close control is labelled 'Cancel' not 'Esc', but pressing Esc dismisses the dialog and restores focus to the trigger. A naive checker sees a focus cycle with no documented exit and wrongly flags a trap; it actually passes because Esc is a standard exit method, so no advice is owed.
mechanism: Modal contains Tab focus correctly; the keydown handler on #dialog closes on Escape and restores focus to #openBtn. Because the exit uses a standard method (Esc), the SC's advice clause is never triggered, so the absence of instructions does not fail it. Verified by probe: opened into dialog, Esc returned focus to #openBtn (inDialog=false).

aspectTitle: Arrow-key / roving-tabindex composite-widget traps (menu, grid, listbox, radiogroup, tablist, slider)
aspectDescription: The SC text and Trusted Tester both name unmodified arrow keys as standard navigation, and the Understanding's calendar-widget example is built on arrow navigation. Composite widgets implemented with roving tabindex commonly capture arrow keys inside the widget; the conformance question is whether Tab/Shift-Tab still moves focus OUT of the widget even when arrows are captured. The corpus contains NO arrow-driven widget at all — it only tests Tab/Shift-Tab on flat lists of buttons. The judgment a human must make is semantic: recognize the construct as a composite widget, understand its expected
scenario: Restaurant online-ordering 'Browse menu' dropdown built as an APG role=menu with roving tabindex; arrows move among dishes but the keydown handler also preventDefault()s Tab/Shift+Tab and remaps them to item movement, so once focus enters the open menu it can never reach the promo field or the checkout button. No Esc, no documented exit.
mechanism: keydown listener on ul[role=menu] has a `case 'Tab': e.preventDefault()` branch that confiscates Tab/Shift+Tab and routes them through the roving-tabindex item mover; arrows are captured legitimately but Tab is also swallowed so focus is confined to the five menuitems with no standard exit and no advised alternate (verified: 6 Tab presses stay on role=menuitem, never reach #promo/#applyBtn).

aspectTitle: Arrow-key / roving-tabindex composite-widget traps (menu, grid, listbox, radiogroup, tablist, slider)
aspectDescription: The SC text and Trusted Tester both name unmodified arrow keys as standard navigation, and the Understanding's calendar-widget example is built on arrow navigation. Composite widgets implemented with roving tabindex commonly capture arrow keys inside the widget; the conformance question is whether Tab/Shift-Tab still moves focus OUT of the widget even when arrows are captured. The corpus contains NO arrow-driven widget at all — it only tests Tab/Shift-Tab on flat lists of buttons. The judgment a human must make is semantic: recognize the construct as a composite widget, understand its expected
scenario: E-commerce headphones store with a custom div role=slider 'Max price' facet. Arrows (and PageUp/Down, Home/End) adjust the price with complete ARIA value semantics, but the thumb keydown handler also captures Tab with preventDefault() 'to prevent accidental value loss when you tab away mid-drag', with no Esc and no instruction, so focus is stranded on the thumb and cannot reach Apply, the brand checkboxes, or the product links.
mechanism: div#thumb[role=slider] keydown handler has a `case 'Tab': e.preventDefault()` branch; the slider legitimately owns ArrowUp/Down/PageUp/Down/Home/End for value changes but also confiscates Tab/Shift+Tab, leaving no standard exit and no advised alternate (verified: ArrowUp changes aria-valuenow so arrows work, while 6 Tab presses keep focus on #thumb and never reach #applyPrice or the checkboxes).

scenario: RTL Arabic article-publishing editor with an APG role=toolbar (Bold/Italic/Underline/List/Link) using roving tabindex and aria-pressed toggles. In RTL, ArrowLeft advances; the handler also captures Tab and the movement WRAPS, so at the last button advancing loops back to the first instead of exiting — a closed within-widget loop with no exit index. The title field and Publish button are unreachable. No Esc, no instruction.
mechanism: div#fmtbar[role=toolbar] keydown handler routes a preventDefault()ed Tab through a wrapping rove() function (index computed as (n+len)%len); because movement wraps, there is no position at which Tab falls through to the next control — it is a within-widget loop trap (distinct from a single self-refocus), and Shift+Tab loops the other way, both confined with no advised exit (verified: 8 Tab presses stay on toolbar buttons, never reach #title/#bodyarea/#publishBtn).

aspectTitle: Multi-element region loop: G21 mechanism #1 (Tab must exit the subset after the final location) where no advice is owed
aspectDescription: G21's first sufficient mechanism is purely behavioral and needs NO advice: ensure that Tab exits the subset of content after it reaches the final navigation location. The distinguishing failure is a within-region LOOP — focus reaches the last control of a sub-section and Tab wraps back to that section's first control instead of progressing to the rest of the page (Trusted Tester 2.b: access restricted to a small section with no way to navigate out of the loop). The corpus's loops are degenerate — Failed 1/2 self-refocus on ONE element, and the documented-exit ping-pong cases all carry advice o
scenario: Garden-centre 'New This Season' page: a 5-card featured carousel (Add-to-basket buttons) sits between header nav and footer nav. The last card's button has a keydown handler that preventDefaults forward Tab and focus()es the first card, walling off the footer links. No advice given.
mechanism: G21 mechanism #1 violated: forward Tab on the region's final control does NOT exit the subset after the final navigation location; it loops 1->2->3->4->5->1 within the carousel, so the footer nav is unreachable by keyboard. Plain Tab is in play so no alternate-method advice is owed — the page fails purely on the behavioural question.

aspectTitle: Required-input / sequential-gate exception: a section that demands interaction before focus progresses is NOT a failure
aspectDescription: Trusted Tester explicitly carves out a non-failure: if a section of a page requires input or interaction before allowing focus to progress to the rest of the page, this is NOT a keyboard trap failure. The corpus has NO form scenario at all — no <form>, <input>, <select>, or <textarea> anywhere — so this exception is never exercised. The judgment is semantic and easy to get wrong: a required-field gate where focus cannot advance until the user completes the field LOOKS like a trap (Tab does not move focus forward) but is conformant; an actual trap is one where focus cannot advance even AFTER th
scenario: Public-library account-signup form: a required email field suppresses a plain forward Tab while the value is not a valid e-mail (so it LOOKS like a trap), then releases focus to the password field, submit button and rest of the page the instant a valid address is typed by keyboard. Shift+Tab is never blocked. Conformant keyboard-satisfiable input gate (PASS boundary variant).
mechanism: A scoped keydown handler on the required #email input calls preventDefault() on a plain forward Tab only while !checkValidity(); once a valid e-mail is entered by keyboard the gate releases and standard Tab advances. The required interaction is keyboard-completable and focus then progresses, exactly matching the TT Test 2.b Note carve-out, so there is no trap.

After the user types a valid UK postcode (BS35 1HJ) by keyboard, every Tab/Shift+Tab/click-away snaps focus back to the field, so focus can never reach the date-of-birth field or Continue button. The input-gate exception requires focus to be ABLE to progress once the interaction is done, which it never can here.

aspectTitle: Documented custom-exit advice that is unreachable or inaccurate beyond the corpus's Ctrl+M-before-trap pattern
aspectDescription: TT Evaluate-Results 1.b requires custom escape keystrokes to be DOCUMENTED AND AVAILABLE, and How-to-Test 3.a/3.b require checking that contextual help discloses the alternate command and that the command actually works. The corpus covers advice-before-trap, advice-within-trap, and a help-link inside the subset (Passed 4/5/6), plus three failure modes (never advised, generic/non-instructive, named-but-broken). But it tests these only on the Ctrl+M-on-flat-buttons template and only with advice that is either plainly present or plainly absent. The uncovered judgment surface is advice REACHABILIT
scenario: County property-tax estimator: a Millage Worksheet loops focus internally; the working custom exit (Ctrl+M) is documented ONLY inside a collapsed <details> placed in DOM/visual order AFTER the trap, so a trapped keyboard user can never reach or open it.
mechanism: Focus is trapped (blur re-focuses the first field); Ctrl+M genuinely exits, but its sole instruction lives in a post-trap collapsed disclosure unreachable from inside the loop — advice present but not reachable within the subset (G21 'accessible manner within the subset' violated by placement).
